**S2. You need to implement an undo/redo system for a document editor using dataclasses.**

> **Answer:**
>
> ```python
> from dataclasses import dataclass, field, replace, asdict
> from typing import List, Optional
> from datetime import datetime
>
> @dataclass(frozen=True)
> class DocumentState:
>     """Immutable document state — each edit creates new state"""
>     title:    str
>     content:  str
>     font:     str   = "Arial"
>     size:     int   = 12
>     bold:     bool  = False
>     italic:   bool  = False
>     version:  int   = 1
>     modified: str   = field(default_factory=lambda: datetime.now().isoformat())
>
> class DocumentEditor:
>     """
>     Document editor with unlimited undo/redo.
>     Uses replace() to create new immutable states.
>     """
>     def __init__(self, initial_content: str, title: str = "Untitled"):
>         self._history: List[DocumentState] = [
>             DocumentState(title=title, content=initial_content)
>         ]
>         self._position: int = 0  # current position in history
>
>     @property
>     def current(self) -> DocumentState:
>         return self._history[self._position]
>
>     def _push_state(self, new_state: DocumentState):
>         """Add state to history, discarding redo history"""
>         # Discard any redo history
>         self._history = self._history[:self._position + 1]
>         # Increment version
>         new_state = replace(new_state,
>                            version=self.current.version + 1,
>                            modified=datetime.now().isoformat())
>         self._history.append(new_state)
>         self._position += 1
>
>     def type_text(self, new_content: str):
>         self._push_state(replace(self.current, content=new_content))
>
>     def rename(self, new_title: str):
>         self._push_state(replace(self.current, title=new_title))
>
>     def format(self, **formatting):
>         """Apply formatting: bold, italic, font, size"""
>         self._push_state(replace(self.current, **formatting))
>
>     def undo(self) -> bool:
>         if self._position > 0:
>             self._position -= 1
>             return True
>         print("Nothing to undo")
>         return False
>
>     def redo(self) -> bool:
>         if self._position < len(self._history) - 1:
>             self._position += 1
>             return True
>         print("Nothing to redo")
>         return False
>
>     def history_summary(self):
>         print(f"\nHistory ({len(self._history)} states, at v{self.current.version}):")
>         for i, state in enumerate(self._history):
>             marker = "→" if i == self._position else " "
>             print(f"  {marker} v{state.version}: '{state.content[:30]}...' "
>                   f"bold={state.bold}")
>
> # Demo
> editor = DocumentEditor("Hello World", "My Document")
>
> editor.type_text("Hello, Python World!")
> editor.format(bold=True, size=14)
> editor.type_text("Hello, Python World! This is great.")
> editor.rename("Python Document")
>
> editor.history_summary()
>
> print(f"\nCurrent: v{editor.current.version} — '{editor.current.content}'")
> editor.undo()
> print(f"After undo: v{editor.current.version} — '{editor.current.content}'")
> editor.undo()
> print(f"After undo: bold={editor.current.bold}")
> editor.redo()
> print(f"After redo: bold={editor.current.bold}")
>
> # Original states are preserved (immutable)
> print(f"\nHistory intact: {len(editor._history)} states")
> ```

**S3. You're building an API that accepts dynamic query filters. Use `make_dataclass()` to validate them.**

> **Answer:**
>
> ```python
> from dataclasses import make_dataclass, field, asdict, fields
> import dataclasses
> from typing import Optional, List, Dict, Any, Type
>
> # Filter schemas per endpoint — loaded from config/DB
> FILTER_SCHEMAS: Dict[str, Dict] = {
>     "users": {
>         "username":   {"type": str,   "required": False, "default": ""},
>         "email":      {"type": str,   "required": False, "default": ""},
>         "is_active":  {"type": bool,  "required": False, "default": True},
>         "age_min":    {"type": int,   "required": False, "default": 0},
>         "age_max":    {"type": int,   "required": False, "default": 150},
>     },
>     "products": {
>         "category":   {"type": str,   "required": False, "default": ""},
>         "price_min":  {"type": float, "required": False, "default": 0.0},
>         "price_max":  {"type": float, "required": False, "default": 999999.0},
>         "in_stock":   {"type": bool,  "required": False, "default": True},
>     }
>
> }
>
> # Cache dynamically created classes
> _filter_classes: Dict[str, Type] = {}
>
> def get_filter_class(endpoint: str) -> Type:
>     """Get or create filter dataclass for endpoint"""
>     if endpoint in _filter_classes:
>         return _filter_classes[endpoint]
>
>     schema = FILTER_SCHEMAS.get(endpoint)
>     if not schema:
>         raise ValueError(f"Unknown endpoint: {endpoint}")
>
>     # Build field list for make_dataclass
>     field_defs = []
>     for field_name, config in schema.items():
>         default = config.get("default", "")
>         field_defs.append((
>             field_name,
>             Optional[config["type"]],
>             field(default=default)
>         ))
>
>     # Create the class
>     cls = make_dataclass(
>         f"{endpoint.title()}Filter",
>         field_defs,
>     )
>     _filter_classes[endpoint] = cls
>     return cls
>
> def parse_filters(endpoint: str, query_params: Dict[str, Any]) -> Any:
>     """Parse and validate query parameters into filter dataclass"""
>     FilterClass = get_filter_class(endpoint)
>
>     # Type-cast query params
>     type_hints = {f.name: f.type for f in fields(FilterClass)}
>     cast_params = {}
>
>     for f in fields(FilterClass):
>         if f.name in query_params:
>             raw  = query_params[f.name]
>             # Get the inner type from Optional[X]
>             inner = getattr(f.type, '__args__', (str,))[0]
>             try:
>                 if inner == bool:
>                     cast_params[f.name] = raw.lower() in ("true","1","yes")
>                 else:
>                     cast_params[f.name] = inner(raw)
>             except (ValueError, AttributeError):
>                 cast_params[f.name] = f.default
>
>     return FilterClass(**cast_params)
>
> # Simulate API requests
> user_params = {"username": "alice", "is_active": "true", "age_min": "25"}
> user_filters = parse_filters("users", user_params)
>
> prod_params = {"category": "electronics", "price_max": "1500.00", "in_stock": "false"}
> prod_filters = parse_filters("products", prod_params)
>
> print(f"User filters   : {user_filters}")
> print(f"Product filters: {prod_filters}")
> print(f"Is dataclass   : {dataclasses.is_dataclass(user_filters)}")
> print(f"As dict        : {asdict(user_filters)}")
>
> # Same class is reused (cached)
> cls1 = get_filter_class("users")
> cls2 = get_filter_class("users")
> print(f"Same class: {cls1 is cls2}")  # True
> ```

sections.title: What is Enum? — Conceptual Interview Questions & Answers
sections.body:
**Q1. What is an Enum and why is it better than using string or integer constants?**

> **5-Year Exp Answer:**
> An Enum (enumeration) is a set of named, immutable constants grouped under a type. Advantages over strings/ints: (1) **Type safety** — `status = OrderStatus.PENDING` is self-documenting; `status = "pendingg"` is a silent bug. (2) **IDE support** — autocomplete, refactoring, go-to-definition all work. (3) **Iteration** — `for s in OrderStatus:` gives all valid values. (4) **Equality** — Enum members are singletons (`is` comparison works). (5) **Namespace** — all related constants in one place, no naming conflicts. (6) **Impossible invalid values** — `OrderStatus("invalid")` raises `ValueError`. In production: I replaced all magic string constants with Enums in a large codebase and caught 15 bugs from typos and inconsistent naming in the first pass.

**Q2. What are the different ways to access an Enum member?**

> **5-Year Exp Answer:**
> Four access patterns: (1) **Direct** — `Color.RED` — most common, use in code logic. (2) **By name** — `Color['RED']` — use when you have a string name (e.g., from config file). (3) **By value** — `Color(1)` — use when you have a value (e.g., from database or API). (4) **Iteration** — `for c in Color:` — use to enumerate all members. Properties: `.name` returns the name string (`'RED'`); `.value` returns the assigned value (`1`). Common gotcha: `Color.RED == 'RED'` is `False` and `Color.RED == 1` is `False` (for regular Enum). Use `Color.RED.value == 1` for value comparison or `Color.RED.name == 'RED'` for name comparison. For value equality: use `IntEnum` or `StrEnum`.

**Q3. What happens when you compare Enum members?**

> **5-Year Exp Answer:**
> Regular `Enum` members use **identity comparison** — two members are equal only if they're the same member. `Color.RED == Color.RED` is `True`. `Color.RED == Color.BLUE` is `False`. `Color.RED == 'RED'` is `False` — Enum is NOT equal to its name. `Color.RED == 1` is `False` — Enum is NOT equal to its value. For ordering (`<`, `>`), regular `Enum` raises `TypeError` — no ordering by default. `IntEnum` changes this: values are integers and support all integer comparisons including `<`, `>`. `is` comparison works for Enum members because each member is a singleton — `Color.RED is Color.RED` is always `True`. Use `is` for Enum comparisons in performance-critical code (slightly faster than `==`).

**Q4. How do you safely convert a string or integer to an Enum without crashing?**

> **5-Year Exp Answer:**
>
> ```python
> from enum import Enum
>
> class Status(Enum):
>     ACTIVE   = "active"
>     INACTIVE = "inactive"
>
> # Direct (raises ValueError if invalid)
> s = Status("active")   # works
> s = Status("unknown")  # raises ValueError!
>
> # Safe conversion patterns:
>
> # Pattern 1: try/except
> def safe_status(value: str) -> Status:
>     try:
>         return Status(value)
>     except ValueError:
>         return Status.INACTIVE  # default
>
> # Pattern 2: dict lookup
> _status_map = {s.value: s for s in Status}
> def from_value(value: str) -> Status:
>     return _status_map.get(value, Status.INACTIVE)
>
> # Pattern 3: hasattr check
> def from_name(name: str) -> Status:
>     return Status[name] if name in Status.__members__ else Status.INACTIVE
>
> # In API handlers, I always use safe conversion:
> user_input = "unknown_status"
> status = safe_status(user_input)
> print(f"Safe: {status.name}")   # INACTIVE (default)
> ```
>
> In production APIs, I always validate enum input before constructing business objects — never let invalid enum values propagate into the domain layer.

**Q5. Can Enum members have methods? Can they have multiple values?**

> **5-Year Exp Answer:**
> Yes to both! Enums are full classes — members can have methods, properties, and classmethods:
>
> ```python
> class Planet(Enum):
>     MERCURY = (3.303e+23, 2.4397e6)  # (mass, radius) — MULTIPLE VALUES!
>     VENUS   = (4.869e+24, 6.0518e6)
>     EARTH   = (5.976e+24, 6.37814e6)
>
>     def __init__(self, mass: float, radius: float):
>         self.mass   = mass
>         self.radius = radius
>
>     @property
>     def surface_gravity(self) -> float:
>         G = 6.67430e-11
>         return G * self.mass / (self.radius ** 2)
>
>     @property
>     def escape_velocity(self) -> float:
>         return (2 * self.surface_gravity * self.radius) ** 0.5
>
> print(Planet.EARTH.surface_gravity)   # ~9.8 m/s²
> print(Planet.EARTH.escape_velocity)   # ~11,186 m/s
> ```
>
> For multiple values, `__init__` receives all values after `self`. The `value` property returns the first one (or the tuple). I use multi-value Enums for: HTTP methods with descriptions, database types with SQL mappings, currencies with symbols and decimal places.

**S1. You have status codes scattered as strings throughout a large codebase. How do you safely migrate to Enums?**

> **Answer:**
>
> ```python
> from enum import Enum
> from typing import Union
>
> class TicketStatus(Enum):
>     OPEN       = "open"
>     IN_PROGRESS= "in_progress"
>     REVIEW     = "review"
>     DONE       = "done"
>     CLOSED     = "closed"
>     CANCELLED  = "cancelled"
>
>     @classmethod
>     def from_legacy(cls, value: Union[str, int, None]) -> "TicketStatus":
>         """
>         Migration helper: convert any legacy format to Enum.
>         Handles: old strings, integers, None, different casings.
>         """
>         if value is None:
>             return cls.OPEN  # default
>
>         # Handle legacy integer codes
>         legacy_int_map = {1:"open", 2:"in_progress", 3:"done", 4:"closed"}
>         if isinstance(value, int):
>             value = legacy_int_map.get(value, "open")
>
>         # Normalize: lowercase, replace spaces with underscores
>         normalized = str(value).lower().replace(" ", "_").replace("-", "_")
>
>         # Try direct match
>         try:
>             return cls(normalized)
>         except ValueError:
>             pass
>
>         # Try name match
>         try:
>             return cls[normalized.upper()]
>         except KeyError:
>             pass
>
>         # Legacy name aliases
>         aliases = {
>             "new":       cls.OPEN,
>             "wip":       cls.IN_PROGRESS,
>             "complete":  cls.DONE,
>             "resolved":  cls.CLOSED,
>             "rejected":  cls.CANCELLED,
>         }
>         return aliases.get(normalized, cls.OPEN)
>
>     @property
>     def is_active(self) -> bool:
>         return self in {self.OPEN, self.IN_PROGRESS, self.REVIEW}
>
>     @property
>     def label(self) -> str:
>         return self.value.replace("_", " ").title()
>
> # Migration test
> legacy_values = ["open", "in_progress", "WIP", "DONE", 3, None,
>                  "complete", "new", "IN PROGRESS", "unknown_value"]
>
> print("Legacy value migration:")
> for val in legacy_values:
>     status = TicketStatus.from_legacy(val)
>     print(f"  {str(val):<20} → {status.name:<15} (active: {status.is_active})")
>
> # Backward compatible serialization
> def serialize_status(status: TicketStatus) -> dict:
>     return {
>         "status":       status.value,    # new format
>         "status_label": status.label,    # human readable
>         # "status_id": legacy_map[status]  # if old clients need int
>     }
>
> print(f"\nSerialized: {serialize_status(TicketStatus.IN_PROGRESS)}")
> ```

sections.title: Enum Types — Conceptual Interview Questions & Answers
sections.body:
**Q1. What is the difference between `Enum`, `IntEnum`, and `StrEnum`?**

> **5-Year Exp Answer:**
> `Enum` is the base class — members are their own type and NOT equal to their values (`Color.RED != "red"`, `Color.RED != 1`). `IntEnum` makes members behave as integers — `Status.ACTIVE == 1` is `True`, sorting and arithmetic work. `StrEnum` (3.11+) or `(str, Enum)` makes members behave as strings — `Direction.NORTH == "north"` is `True`, string methods work directly. When to use each: `Enum` — when you want strict type separation (prevent accidental string/int comparisons). `IntEnum` — when interfacing with databases that store integers, sorting by value, or legacy code expecting ints. `StrEnum` — API field names, JSON keys, database column names, config keys where string comparison is natural. I use `StrEnum` for API response field names — they work directly as JSON keys without `.value` conversion.

**Q2. What is `auto()` and how can you customize it?**

> **5-Year Exp Answer:**
> `auto()` automatically generates a value for an Enum member so you don't hardcode numbers. Default behavior: starts at 1, increments by 1. Customized by overriding `_generate_next_value_(name, start, count, last_values)` as a static method: `name` = member name, `start` = starting value, `count` = how many values assigned so far, `last_values` = list of previous values. Common customizations: (1) Uppercase strings: `return name.upper()`. (2) Lowercase strings: `return name.lower()`. (3) Powers of 2 for flags: `return 2 ** count`. (4) From a list: `return my_list[count]`. I use custom `auto()` to generate `StrEnum` values from names automatically — no need to maintain name-value pairs that always match.

**Q3. What is `Flag` and when do you use it instead of `Enum`?**

> **5-Year Exp Answer:**
> `Flag` allows members to be **combined** using bitwise operators (`|`, `&`, `~`, `^`). Each member is a power of 2, so any combination has a unique value. Use `Flag` when: (1) An entity can have multiple states simultaneously. (2) You're modeling permissions (read+write+delete). (3) You're modeling tags/categories (multiple categories). (4) You're interfacing with C/OS bitfield APIs. Regular `Enum` = mutually exclusive states (order is PENDING _or_ SHIPPED, not both). `Flag` = combinable properties (user has READ _and_ WRITE _and_ DELETE permissions). Common uses: Unix file permissions, HTTP capabilities, feature flags, user role permissions. `IntFlag` combines Flag with integer behavior — useful for OS-level APIs.

**Q4. How do you iterate and filter Enum members?**

> **5-Year Exp Answer:**
>
> ```python
> from enum import Enum
>
> class Status(Enum):
>     ACTIVE   = "active"
>     INACTIVE = "inactive"
>     PENDING  = "pending"
>     DELETED  = "deleted"
>
> # Iterate all
> all_statuses = list(Status)
> all_values   = [s.value for s in Status]
> all_names    = [s.name for s in Status]
>
> # Filter by condition
> active_states = [s for s in Status if s != Status.DELETED]
>
> # Build lookup maps
> by_value = {s.value: s for s in Status}  # {"active": Status.ACTIVE, ...}
> by_name  = {s.name: s for s in Status}   # {"ACTIVE": Status.ACTIVE, ...}
>
> # In production, I pre-build these maps once at module level
> # for O(1) lookups instead of O(n) iteration:
> STATUS_BY_VALUE = {s.value: s for s in Status}
>
> def get_status(value: str) -> Status:
>     return STATUS_BY_VALUE.get(value, Status.INACTIVE)
> ```
>
> `len(Status)` gives member count. `Status.__members__` is an ordered dict of all members including aliases. Filtering is just list comprehension over the Enum.

**Q5. What are Enum aliases and how do you work with them?**

> **5-Year Exp Answer:**
> Enum aliases occur when two members have the same value — the second becomes an alias for the first:
>
> ```python
> class Color(Enum):
>     RED    = 1
>     ROUGE  = 1   # alias for RED! (same value)
>     GREEN  = 2
>     BLUE   = 3
>
> Color.RED is Color.ROUGE  # True — they're the same member!
> Color['ROUGE']            # Color.RED (canonical name)
> list(Color)               # [RED, GREEN, BLUE] — ROUGE not listed!
> Color.__members__         # includes ROUGE as key
> ```
>
> To prevent aliases (raise error if duplicate values): use `@unique` decorator from `enum`:
>
> ```python
> from enum import Enum, unique
>
> @unique
> class StrictColor(Enum):
>     RED   = 1
>     ROUGE = 1   # ValueError: duplicate values! ROUGE: 1
> ```
>
> I always use `@unique` in production code — accidental aliases cause confusing behavior. The only time I intentionally use aliases is when supporting multiple names for backward compatibility.

**S2. You need to interface with a legacy API that uses integer status codes. How do you use IntEnum?**

> **Answer:**
>
> ```python
> from enum import IntEnum
> from dataclasses import dataclass
> from typing import Optional, Dict, Any
> import json
>
> class LegacyStatus(IntEnum):
>     """Maps legacy integer codes to meaningful names"""
>     SUCCESS         = 0
>     PENDING         = 1
>     IN_PROGRESS     = 2
>     COMPLETED       = 3
>     FAILED          = 4
>     PARTIALLY_DONE  = 5
>     CANCELLED       = 99
>     UNKNOWN         = -1
>
>     @property
>     def is_terminal(self) -> bool:
>         return self in {self.COMPLETED, self.FAILED, self.CANCELLED}
>
>     @property
>     def needs_retry(self) -> bool:
>         return self in {self.FAILED}
>
>     @property
>     def message(self) -> str:
>         messages = {
>             0: "Operation completed successfully",
>             1: "Waiting to be processed",
>             2: "Currently being processed",
>             3: "Done",
>             4: "Operation failed",
>             99: "Operation was cancelled",
>         }
>         return messages.get(self.value, "Unknown status")
>
>     @classmethod
>     def safe_from_code(cls, code: int) -> "LegacyStatus":
>         try:
>             return cls(code)
>         except ValueError:
>             return cls.UNKNOWN
>
> @dataclass
> class LegacyAPIResponse:
>     job_id:     str
>     status_code:int   # raw from API
>     data:       Dict[str, Any]
>
>     @property
>     def status(self) -> LegacyStatus:
>         return LegacyStatus.safe_from_code(self.status_code)
>
> def process_legacy_response(raw_json: str):
>     """Process legacy API response using IntEnum"""
>     data = json.loads(raw_json)
>
>     response = LegacyAPIResponse(
>         job_id     = data["job_id"],
>         status_code= data["status"],   # raw int from API
>         data       = data.get("data", {})
>     )
>
>     status = response.status
>     print(f"Job   : {response.job_id}")
>     print(f"Status: {status.name} ({status.value}) — {status.message}")
>     print(f"Done  : {status.is_terminal}")
>
>     # IntEnum lets you do integer comparisons!
>     if status >= LegacyStatus.FAILED:
>         print(f"⚠️  High status code: {status.value}")
>
>     if status.needs_retry:
>         print(f"🔄 Should retry this job")
>
>     return status
>
> # Simulate legacy API responses
> responses = [
>     '{"job_id":"J001","status":0,"data":{"result":"done"}}',
>     '{"job_id":"J002","status":4,"data":{}}',
>     '{"job_id":"J003","status":999,"data":{}}',  # unknown code
> ]
>
> for r in responses:
>     print(f"\n{'='*40}")
>     process_legacy_response(r)
> ```

**S3. Build a feature flag system using StrEnum and Flag.**

> **Answer:**
>
> ```python
> from enum import Flag, auto
> from dataclasses import dataclass, field
> from typing import Dict, Set
>
> class Feature(Flag):
>     """Feature flags — can be combined"""
>     NONE              = 0
>     DARK_MODE         = auto()
>     BETA_DASHBOARD    = auto()
>     AI_ASSISTANT      = auto()
>     ADVANCED_ANALYTICS= auto()
>     EXPORT_PDF        = auto()
>     MULTI_CURRENCY    = auto()
>     API_V2            = auto()
>     REAL_TIME_UPDATES = auto()
>
>     # Tier bundles
>     FREE_FEATURES = DARK_MODE | EXPORT_PDF
>     PRO_FEATURES  = FREE_FEATURES | BETA_DASHBOARD | ADVANCED_ANALYTICS | MULTI_CURRENCY
>     ENTERPRISE    = PRO_FEATURES | AI_ASSISTANT | API_V2 | REAL_TIME_UPDATES
>
> @dataclass
> class FeatureFlagService:
>     """Manages feature flags per user/account"""
>     _user_flags:    Dict[str, Feature] = field(default_factory=dict)
>     _account_flags: Dict[str, Feature] = field(default_factory=dict)
>
>     def enable(self, user_id: str, feature: Feature):
>         self._user_flags[user_id] = self._user_flags.get(user_id, Feature.NONE) | feature
>
>     def disable(self, user_id: str, feature: Feature):
>         current = self._user_flags.get(user_id, Feature.NONE)
>         self._user_flags[user_id] = current & ~feature
>
>     def set_tier(self, user_id: str, tier: str):
>         tier_map = {
>             "free":       Feature.FREE_FEATURES,
>             "pro":        Feature.PRO_FEATURES,
>             "enterprise": Feature.ENTERPRISE,
>         }
>         self._user_flags[user_id] = tier_map.get(tier, Feature.FREE_FEATURES)
>
>     def is_enabled(self, user_id: str, feature: Feature) -> bool:
>         user_features = self._user_flags.get(user_id, Feature.NONE)
>         return feature in user_features
>
>     def get_enabled(self, user_id: str) -> Set[str]:
>         user_features = self._user_flags.get(user_id, Feature.NONE)
>         return {f.name for f in Feature if f.value and f in user_features
>                 and not any(x in f.name for x in ["FEATURES","ENTERPRISE"])}
>
> # Demo
> svc = FeatureFlagService()
>
> svc.set_tier("alice", "pro")
> svc.set_tier("bob",   "free")
> svc.enable("bob", Feature.AI_ASSISTANT)  # special access
>
> for user in ["alice", "bob"]:
>     features = svc.get_enabled(user)
>     print(f"\n{user}'s features: {features}")
>     print(f"  AI Assistant  : {svc.is_enabled(user, Feature.AI_ASSISTANT)}")
>     print(f"  API V2        : {svc.is_enabled(user, Feature.API_V2)}")
> ```

sections.title: What is Pydantic? — Conceptual Interview Questions & Answers
sections.body:
**Q1. What is Pydantic and how is it different from Python dataclasses?**

> **5-Year Exp Answer:**
> Pydantic is a data validation and parsing library that uses Python type hints to enforce data integrity. Key differences from dataclasses: (1) **Validation** — Pydantic validates every field on creation; dataclasses don't validate at all without manual `__post_init__` code. (2) **Type coercion** — Pydantic converts `"42"` to `42` for an `int` field; dataclasses store `"42"` as a string without complaint. (3) **Error handling** — Pydantic raises `ValidationError` with detailed field-by-field error info; dataclasses raise `TypeError` only for wrong argument count. (4) **JSON schema** — Pydantic auto-generates JSON Schema and OpenAPI specs; dataclasses have nothing. (5) **Serialization** — Pydantic's `model_dump()` handles nested models, datetime, Enum automatically. I use dataclasses for internal domain objects where I control the data. I use Pydantic for API boundaries, external data parsing, and configuration.

**Q2. What is automatic type coercion in Pydantic and when can it cause problems?**

> **5-Year Exp Answer:**
> Pydantic v2 in "lax" mode (default) attempts to coerce compatible types: `"42"` → `42` (str to int), `"true"` → `True` (str to bool), `"2024-01-15"` → `date` object (str to date), `1` → `True` (int to bool). Useful for: parsing JSON (everything is strings), form data, query parameters. Potential problems: (1) `bool` coercion — `"0"` → `True` (non-empty string!), `0` → `False`. This surprises many developers. (2) `int` coercion from `float` — `3.7` → `3` (truncation, not rounding). (3) Silently accepting wrong types from API clients who should fix their code. Fix: use `model_config = ConfigDict(strict=True)` — no coercion, values must be exact types. For payment systems and financial apps, I always use strict mode to prevent silent data corruption.

**Q3. What is `ValidationError` and what information does it contain?**

> **5-Year Exp Answer:**
> `ValidationError` is raised when Pydantic fails to validate a model. It contains a list of errors, each with: `loc` (field location as tuple, e.g., `('address', 'zipcode')`), `msg` (human-readable error message), `type` (machine-readable error code like `'int_parsing'`, `'missing'`, `'string_too_short'`), `url` (Pydantic docs link for that error type), `input` (the value that failed). Access errors with `e.errors()` (list of dicts) or `e.error_count()` (count). In production APIs, I transform `ValidationError` to user-friendly 422 responses:
>
> ```python
> except ValidationError as e:
>     return {
>         "status": 422,
>         "errors": [
>             {"field": ".".join(str(l) for l in err["loc"]),
>              "message": err["msg"]}
>             for err in e.errors()
>         ]
>     }
> ```
>
> Never expose raw Pydantic error objects to API clients — they may contain internal implementation details.

**Q4. How does Pydantic handle nested models?**

> **5-Year Exp Answer:**
> Pydantic handles nested models automatically. A field typed as another `BaseModel` subclass accepts either: a dict (auto-converted), a model instance (used as-is), or a compatible object with `from_attributes=True`. Nested validation: all nested models are validated recursively. Error locations reflect the nesting: `('address', 'zipcode', 'too_short')`. Serialization: `model_dump()` recursively converts nested models to dicts. `model_dump_json()` serializes the entire tree to JSON. Partial updates with nested models require `model_copy(update={"address": new_address})`. Real-world pattern I use: separate Request, Response, and Domain models — Request model validates API input, Domain model has business logic, Response model controls exactly what's returned (never expose internal fields):
>
> ```python
> class CreateOrderRequest(BaseModel): ...   # validates input
> class Order(BaseModel): ...                 # domain logic
> class OrderResponse(BaseModel): ...        # controls output shape
> ```

**Q5. What is the difference between Pydantic v1 and v2?**

> **5-Year Exp Answer:**
> Pydantic v2 (2023+) is a complete rewrite in Rust — 5-50x faster than v1. Key API changes: (1) `@validator` → `@field_validator` (different signature and mode parameter). (2) `@root_validator` → `@model_validator`. (3) `class Config` → `model_config = ConfigDict(...)`. (4) `.dict()` → `.model_dump()`. (5) `.json()` → `.model_dump_json()`. (6) `.parse_obj()` → `.model_validate()`. (7) `orm_mode=True` → `from_attributes=True`. (8) `update_forward_refs()` → usually not needed in v2. (9) `schema()` → `model_json_schema()`. Migration: use `pydantic.v1` compatibility import during migration. Most breaking changes are in validators — v2 validators receive different arguments. In production, I used `bump-pydantic` tool for automated migration. New projects should always start with v2.

sections.title: What is Pydantic? — Scenario-Based Interview Questions & Answers
sections.body:
**S1. Your API is receiving malformed data from a third-party service. How do you use Pydantic to safely parse it?**

> **Answer:**
>
> ```python
> from pydantic import BaseModel, Field, field_validator, model_validator
> from typing import Optional, List, Any
> from datetime import datetime
>
> class ThirdPartyProduct(BaseModel):
>     """
>     Tolerant parser for messy third-party API data.
>     Handles: missing fields, wrong types, null values, inconsistent formats.
>     """
>     # Use aliases for mismatched field names
>     model_config = {"populate_by_name": True}
>
>     # Third party uses 'prod_id' but we want 'product_id'
>     product_id: str = Field(..., alias="prod_id")
>     name:       str = Field(..., alias="product_name")
>     price:      Optional[float] = Field(None, alias="unit_price")
>     quantity:   int = Field(0, alias="qty")
>     category:   str = Field("unknown", alias="cat")
>     tags:       List[str] = Field(default_factory=list)
>     created_at: Optional[datetime] = None
>
>     @field_validator("price", mode="before")
>     @classmethod
>     def parse_price(cls, v: Any) -> Optional[float]:
>         """Handle: None, '$9.99', '9,99', 9.99"""
>         if v is None:
>             return None
>         if isinstance(v, (int, float)):
>             return float(v)
>         if isinstance(v, str):
>             # Remove currency symbols, spaces, replace comma-decimal
>             cleaned = v.replace("$","").replace("€","").replace(" ","")
>             cleaned = cleaned.replace(",",".")  # European format
>             try:
>                 return float(cleaned)
>             except ValueError:
>                 return None
>         return None
>
>     @field_validator("quantity", mode="before")
>     @classmethod
>     def parse_quantity(cls, v: Any) -> int:
>         """Handle: None, '5', 5.0, '5 pcs'"""
>         if v is None:
>             return 0
>         if isinstance(v, bool):
>             return int(v)
>         if isinstance(v, float):
>             return int(v)
>         if isinstance(v, str):
>             # Extract first number from string
>             import re
>             match = re.search(r'\d+', v)
>             return int(match.group()) if match else 0
>         return int(v)
>
>     @field_validator("tags", mode="before")
>     @classmethod
>     def parse_tags(cls, v: Any) -> List[str]:
>         """Handle: None, 'tag1,tag2', ['tag1','tag2'], 'single'"""
>         if v is None:
>             return []
>         if isinstance(v, list):
>             return [str(t).strip() for t in v if t]
>         if isinstance(v, str):
>             return [t.strip() for t in v.split(",") if t.strip()]
>         return []
>
>     @field_validator("created_at", mode="before")
>     @classmethod
>     def parse_date(cls, v: Any) -> Optional[datetime]:
>         """Handle multiple date formats"""
>         if v is None:
>             return None
>         if isinstance(v, datetime):
>             return v
>         date_formats = [
>             "%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%S",
>             "%Y-%m-%d %H:%M:%S",
>             "%d/%m/%Y",
>             "%m-%d-%Y",
>             "%Y-%m-%d",
>         ]
>         for fmt in date_formats:
>             try:
>                 return datetime.strptime(str(v), fmt)
>             except ValueError:
>                 continue
>         return None
>
> # Simulate messy third-party data
> messy_records = [
>     {
>         "prod_id": "P001", "product_name": "Laptop Pro",
>         "unit_price": "$1,299.99", "qty": "5 pcs",
>         "cat": "electronics", "tags": "laptop,portable,pro",
>         "created_at": "15/01/2024"
>     },
>     {
>         "prod_id": "P002", "product_name": "USB Cable",
>         "unit_price": None, "qty": 10.0,
>         "cat": "accessories", "tags": None,
>         "created_at": None
>     },
>     {
>         "prod_id": "P003", "product_name": "Monitor",
>         "unit_price": "449,00", "qty": "3",   # European price format!
>         "cat": "electronics", "tags": ["monitor", "4K", "gaming"],
>         "created_at": "2024-01-17T09:00:00"
>     },
> ]
>
> print("Parsing messy third-party data:")
> for record in messy_records:
>     try:
>         product = ThirdPartyProduct.model_validate(record)
>         print(f"\n  ✅ {product.product_id}: {product.name}")
>         print(f"     Price: {product.price}  Qty: {product.quantity}")
>         print(f"     Tags : {product.tags}")
>         print(f"     Date : {product.created_at}")
>     except Exception as e:
>         print(f"\n  ❌ Failed: {e}")
> ```

**S2 & S3** — Covered in subsequent chapters with validators and config.

sections.title: Field Types & Validation — Conceptual Interview Questions & Answers
sections.body:
**Q1. What is the difference between `gt`, `ge`, `lt`, `le` in Pydantic Field?**

> **5-Year Exp Answer:**
> These are number comparison constraints: `gt` = **g**reater **t**han (strict, excludes the value itself), `ge` = **g**reater than or **e**qual (inclusive), `lt` = **l**ess **t**han (strict), `le` = **l**ess than or **e**qual (inclusive). Example: `Field(gt=0)` means value must be > 0, so 0 itself is rejected. `Field(ge=0)` means 0 is acceptable. For price: `Field(gt=0, le=999999)` — positive, up to million. For percentage: `Field(ge=0.0, le=100.0)` — 0-100 inclusive. For age: `Field(ge=0, le=150)` — 0 and 150 both valid. I use `gt=0` for prices and quantities (zero doesn't make business sense), `ge=0` for counts and scores (zero is valid).

**Q2. What is the `alias` parameter in Field() and when do you use it?**

> **5-Year Exp Answer:**
> `alias` specifies a different name for the field in input/output data (JSON, dicts). The Python attribute uses the field name, but serialization/deserialization uses the alias. Use cases: (1) **Naming convention mismatch** — your Python uses `snake_case`, API uses `camelCase`. (2) **Reserved words** — field named `type` or `class` conflicts with Python keywords: `type_: str = Field(..., alias="type")`. (3) **Legacy API compatibility** — API uses old names, your code uses clean names. In v2: `validation_alias` (input only), `serialization_alias` (output only), `alias` (both). To accept BOTH alias and field name: `model_config = {"populate_by_name": True}`. To always output with alias: `model.model_dump(by_alias=True)`.

**Q3. What is `Annotated` and how does it help with reusable constraints?**

> **5-Year Exp Answer:**
> `Annotated[T, metadata]` from `typing` attaches metadata to a type without changing it. Pydantic uses this metadata for validation. It enables reusable type aliases:
>
> ```python
> # Define once
> PositiveFloat = Annotated[float, Field(gt=0)]
> EmailStr      = Annotated[str, AfterValidator(validate_email)]
>
> # Use everywhere — DRY principle!
> class User(BaseModel):
>     salary:   PositiveFloat   # same constraints everywhere
>     email:    EmailStr
>
> class Product(BaseModel):
>     price:    PositiveFloat   # reused!
>     cost:     PositiveFloat   # reused!
> ```
>
> Benefits: (1) Single source of truth for constraints. (2) Change constraint in one place, applies everywhere. (3) Self-documenting — type name expresses constraint. (4) Composable — `Annotated[Annotated[str, Field(min_length=1)], Field(max_length=100)]`. I create a `types.py` module with all reusable Annotated types for the entire project.

**Q4. How do you exclude sensitive fields from serialization?**

> **5-Year Exp Answer:**
> Multiple approaches: (1) `Field(exclude=True)` — always excluded from `model_dump()`. Use for: internal fields, passwords (after hashing), audit fields. (2) `model_dump(exclude={"password", "ssn"})` — exclude at call time. Flexible but error-prone. (3) `model_dump(include={"safe_field1", "safe_field2"})` — whitelist approach — safer! (4) Separate Request/Response models — Response model simply doesn't have the field at all. Best practice I follow: create explicit Response models that only contain what should be returned:
>
> ```python
> class UserDB(BaseModel):     # internal — has all fields
>     password_hash: str
>     ssn_hash: str
>     ...
>
> class UserResponse(BaseModel): # public — only safe fields
>     user_id: str
>     username: str
>     email: str
>     # NO password_hash, NO ssn!
> ```
>
> Never rely on `exclude=True` alone for security — a code change could accidentally expose it. Separate models are the safest approach.

**Q5. How does `multiple_of` constraint work and when is it useful?**

> **5-Year Exp Answer:**
> `Field(multiple_of=N)` validates that the value is a multiple of N — i.e., `value % N == 0`. Useful for: (1) **Precision control** — `multiple_of=0.01` ensures max 2 decimal places (though `Decimal` with `decimal_places=2` is better for money). (2) **Lot sizes** — stocks traded in lots of 10: `Field(multiple_of=10)`. (3) **Page sizes** — must be multiple of 5: `Field(multiple_of=5)`. (4) **Weight** — `multiple_of=0.001` for precision to 1 gram. (5) **Memory sizes** — must be power of 2 (with custom validator). For financial precision, I always use `Decimal` with `decimal_places=2` rather than float with `multiple_of` — floating point arithmetic makes `multiple_of` unreliable for non-integer multiples.

sections.title: Field Types & Validation — Scenario-Based Interview Questions & Answers
sections.body:
**S1. Design validation models for an e-commerce checkout API.**

> **Answer:**
>
> ```python
> from pydantic import BaseModel, Field, field_validator
> from typing import Annotated, List, Optional, Literal
> from decimal import Decimal
> from datetime import date
>
> # Reusable types
> Money           = Annotated[Decimal, Field(ge=0, decimal_places=2)]
> PositiveMoney   = Annotated[Decimal, Field(gt=0, decimal_places=2)]
> Percentage      = Annotated[float,   Field(ge=0.0, le=100.0)]
>
> class CartItem(BaseModel):
>     product_id: str  = Field(..., min_length=1)
>     variant_id: Optional[str] = None
>     quantity:   int  = Field(..., ge=1, le=999)
>     unit_price: PositiveMoney
>
>     @computed_field
>     @property
>     def subtotal(self) -> Decimal:
>         return self.unit_price * self.quantity
>
> class ShippingAddress(BaseModel):
>     full_name:   str = Field(..., min_length=2, max_length=100)
>     street_line1:str = Field(..., min_length=5, max_length=200)
>     street_line2:Optional[str] = Field(None, max_length=200)
>     city:        str = Field(..., min_length=1, max_length=100)
>     state:       str = Field(..., min_length=2, max_length=50)
>     postal_code: str = Field(..., pattern=r'^\d{5}(-\d{4})?$')
>     country:     str = Field("US", min_length=2, max_length=2)  # ISO 2-letter
>
> class CreditCard(BaseModel):
>     # Never store real card number — accept token only!
>     token:      str  = Field(..., min_length=10, description="Payment processor token")
>     last_four:  str  = Field(..., pattern=r'^\d{4}$')
>     expiry_month: int = Field(..., ge=1, le=12)
>     expiry_year:  int = Field(..., ge=2024, le=2040)
>     cardholder:  str  = Field(..., min_length=2, max_length=100)
>
>     @field_validator("expiry_year", "expiry_month")
>     @classmethod
>     def validate_not_expired(cls, v, info):
>         today = date.today()
>         if info.field_name == "expiry_year" and v < today.year:
>             raise ValueError("Card is expired")
>         return v
>
> class CheckoutRequest(BaseModel):
>     cart_id:          str
>     items:            List[CartItem]  = Field(..., min_length=1, max_length=50)
>     shipping_address: ShippingAddress
>     payment:          CreditCard
>     coupon_code:      Optional[str]   = Field(None, max_length=20)
>     gift_message:     Optional[str]   = Field(None, max_length=500)
>     save_card:        bool            = False
>
>     @computed_field
>     @property
>     def subtotal(self) -> Decimal:
>         return sum(item.subtotal for item in self.items)
>
>     @computed_field
>     @property
>     def item_count(self) -> int:
>         return sum(item.quantity for item in self.items)
>
> class CheckoutResponse(BaseModel):
>     order_id:       str
>     status:         Literal["confirmed", "pending", "failed"]
>     total_amount:   PositiveMoney
>     estimated_delivery: date
>     confirmation_email: str
>
> from pydantic import computed_field
>
> # Test
> try:
>     checkout = CheckoutRequest(
>         cart_id="CART-001",
>         items=[
>             CartItem(product_id="P1", quantity=2, unit_price="49.99"),
>             CartItem(product_id="P2", quantity=1, unit_price="19.99"),
>         ],
>         shipping_address=ShippingAddress(
>             full_name="Alice Johnson",
>             street_line1="123 Main Street",
>             city="New York", state="NY",
>             postal_code="10001"
>         ),
>         payment=CreditCard(
>             token="tok_visa_test_123456789",
>             last_four="4242",
>             expiry_month=12,
>             expiry_year=2027,
>             cardholder="Alice Johnson"
>         )
>     )
>     print(f"✅ Checkout valid")
>     print(f"  Items   : {checkout.item_count}")
>     print(f"  Subtotal: ${checkout.subtotal}")
> except Exception as e:
>     print(f"❌ Error: {e}")
> ```

sections.title: Model Configuration — Conceptual Interview Questions & Answers
sections.body:
**Q1. What is the difference between `strict=True` and default lax mode in Pydantic?**

> **5-Year Exp Answer:**
> In lax mode (default), Pydantic tries to coerce values: `"42"` → `42`, `"true"` → `True`, `"2024-01-15"` → `date`. In strict mode (`ConfigDict(strict=True)` or `Field(strict=True)`), NO coercion — types must match exactly. `"42"` for an `int` field raises `ValidationError`. Use strict when: (1) Payment systems where silent number truncation is dangerous. (2) Internal service communication where types should already be correct. (3) Security-critical validation where coercion might bypass checks. Use lax when: (1) Parsing HTTP request data (everything comes as strings). (2) Parsing JSON from external APIs. (3) Processing form data. I use lax at API entry points (input from external world) and strict for internal domain models.

**Q2. What is `from_attributes=True` and why is it essential for ORM integration?**

> **5-Year Exp Answer:**
> `from_attributes=True` (formerly `orm_mode=True` in v1) allows Pydantic to read data from objects using `getattr()` instead of dict key access. Without it: Pydantic only reads from dicts. With it: Pydantic can read SQLAlchemy models, Django models, or any object with attributes. Why essential: ORMs return objects, not dicts. `model_validate(orm_object)` requires `from_attributes=True`. Pattern in FastAPI:
>
> ```python
> # SQLAlchemy model
> class UserDB(Base):
>     __tablename__ = "users"
>     id = Column(Integer, primary_key=True)
>     email = Column(String)
>
> # Pydantic response model
> class UserResponse(BaseModel):
>     model_config = ConfigDict(from_attributes=True)
>     id: int
>     email: str
>
> # In endpoint:
> db_user = session.get(UserDB, user_id)
> return UserResponse.model_validate(db_user)  # reads attributes!
> ```
>
> Without `from_attributes=True`, you'd have to manually convert: `UserResponse(**db_user.__dict__)` which is error-prone.

**Q3. What does `extra="forbid"` do and when should you use it?**

> **5-Year Exp Answer:**
> `extra="forbid"` raises `ValidationError` if the input contains any fields not defined in the model. Options: `"ignore"` (default) — silently drops extra fields. `"allow"` — keeps extra in `__pydantic_extra__`. `"forbid"` — raises error. Use `extra="forbid"` for: (1) **Strict API contracts** — detect when client sends wrong/misspelled fields. (2) **Security** — prevent parameter pollution attacks. (3) **Configuration models** — catch typos in config files early. (4) **Internal service contracts** — both sides must agree on exact schema. Avoid `extra="forbid"` for: (1) Parsing third-party APIs that add new fields you don't control. (2) Webhook payloads that may have varying fields. (3) Flexible data models. I use `forbid` for all my Request models (I control what clients send) and `ignore` for Response parsers from external APIs.

**Q4. What does `use_enum_values=True` do and when do you need it?**

> **5-Year Exp Answer:**
> `use_enum_values=True` stores the Enum's `.value` (the raw string/int) instead of the Enum member object. Without it: `model.status` returns `<Status.ACTIVE: 'active'>`. With it: `model.status` returns `'active'`. Use when: (1) JSON serialization — enum members don't serialize naturally, values do. (2) Database storage — you store the value, not the enum object. (3) Comparison with raw strings — `user.role == "admin"` works directly. (4) Template rendering — string values render cleanly. Trade-off: with `use_enum_values=True`, you lose enum type information — can't do `isinstance(user.role, UserRole)`. For APIs, I use `use_enum_values=True` + `StrEnum` so values ARE strings naturally, giving the best of both worlds.

**Q5. What is `frozen=True` in Pydantic config and how does it differ from dataclass frozen?**

> **5-Year Exp Answer:**
> `model_config = ConfigDict(frozen=True)` makes Pydantic model instances immutable — setting attributes after creation raises `ValidationError`. Similar to `@dataclass(frozen=True)` but with Pydantic's validation. Also enables `__hash__` so models can be used as dict keys or in sets. Differences from dataclass frozen: (1) Pydantic validates the type of assigned values; dataclass just prevents assignment. (2) Pydantic's `model_copy(update={...})` creates validated immutable copies; dataclass uses `replace()`. (3) Pydantic frozen raises `ValidationError`, dataclass raises `FrozenInstanceError`. Use case: value objects (Money, Address, Coordinate) that should never change after creation. I use frozen Pydantic models for event objects in event-driven architecture — events should be immutable records of what happened.

sections.title: Model Configuration — Scenario-Based Interview Questions & Answers
sections.body:
**S1. You're integrating Pydantic with SQLAlchemy for a FastAPI application. How do you configure the models?**

> **Answer:**
>
> ```python
> from pydantic import BaseModel, ConfigDict, Field, computed_field
> from typing import Optional, List
> from datetime import datetime
>
> # ── Base Models ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────
> class BaseSchema(BaseModel):
>     """Base for all Pydantic schemas — common config"""
>     model_config = ConfigDict(
>         from_attributes=True,    # works with SQLAlchemy models
>         populate_by_name=True,   # accept both alias and field name
>         str_strip_whitespace=True,
>         use_enum_values=True,
>     )
>
> # ── Request Schemas (strict input validation) ─────────────────────────
> class UserCreate(BaseSchema):
>     model_config = ConfigDict(
>         from_attributes=True,
>         extra="forbid",          # no extra fields in requests!
>         str_strip_whitespace=True,
>     )
>     username: str = Field(..., min_length=3, max_length=50)
>     email:    str = Field(..., min_length=5, max_length=255)
>     password: str = Field(..., min_length=8, exclude=True)
>     role:     str = "user"
>
> class UserUpdate(BaseSchema):
>     model_config = ConfigDict(from_attributes=True, extra="forbid")
>     username: Optional[str] = Field(None, min_length=3, max_length=50)
>     email:    Optional[str] = Field(None, min_length=5, max_length=255)
>     role:     Optional[str] = None
>     is_active:Optional[bool]= None
>
> # ── Response Schemas (control what's returned) ────────────────────────
> class UserResponse(BaseSchema):
>     """What API returns — never includes password"""
>     user_id:    int
>     username:   str
>     email:      str
>     role:       str
>     is_active:  bool
>     created_at: datetime
>     updated_at: datetime
>
>     # Computed fields from ORM relationships
>     @computed_field
>     @property
>     def display_role(self) -> str:
>         return self.role.replace("_", " ").title()
>
> class UserWithPosts(UserResponse):
>     """Extended response including related data"""
>     post_count: int = 0
>     recent_posts: List[dict] = []
>
> # ── Simulated ORM usage ────────────────────────────────────────────────
> class FakeUserDB:
>     """Simulates SQLAlchemy ORM object"""
>     def __init__(self, **kwargs):
>         for k, v in kwargs.items():
>             setattr(self, k, v)
>
> # Simulate DB query result
> db_user = FakeUserDB(
>     user_id=1, username="alice", email="alice@example.com",
>     role="admin", is_active=True, password_hash="hashed!",
>     created_at=datetime.now(), updated_at=datetime.now(),
>     internal_audit_id="AUD-001"  # internal field — NOT in response!
> )
>
> # Convert ORM → Pydantic (from_attributes=True makes this work)
> user_resp = UserResponse.model_validate(db_user)
> print(f"User    : {user_resp.username}")
> print(f"Role    : {user_resp.role}")
> print(f"Display : {user_resp.display_role}")
>
> # password_hash and internal_audit_id NOT in response
> resp_dict = user_resp.model_dump()
> print(f"\nNo password_hash : {'password_hash' not in resp_dict}")
> print(f"No internal_audit: {'internal_audit_id' not in resp_dict}")
> print(f"Response keys    : {list(resp_dict.keys())}")
> ```

sections.title: Validators — Conceptual Interview Questions & Answers
sections.body:
**Q1. What is the difference between `@field_validator` and `@model_validator`?**

> **5-Year Exp Answer:**
> `@field_validator("field_name")` validates/transforms a single field in isolation — it only sees that field's value. `@model_validator` validates the entire model — it has access to ALL fields and can check cross-field relationships. Execution order: (1) `@model_validator(mode="before")` — first, with raw input dict. (2) Field validators — field by field. (3) `@model_validator(mode="after")` — last, with fully validated model instance. Use `@field_validator` for: single-field format validation (email, phone, URL), transformation/normalization, individual business rules. Use `@model_validator` for: cross-field validation (password == confirm_password), conditional requirements (if payment_type=="card" then card_number required), computed fields that depend on multiple inputs.

**Q2. What does `mode="before"` vs `mode="after"` mean in validators?**

> **5-Year Exp Answer:**
> `mode="before"`: validator runs BEFORE Pydantic's type parsing. The input `v` is RAW — could be string, dict, list, None. Use for: parsing/transforming input from external sources, handling multiple input formats (date strings in various formats), cleaning before type conversion. `mode="after"`: validator runs AFTER Pydantic converts the type. `v` is guaranteed to be the correct Python type (`int`, `float`, `date`, etc.). Use for: business rule validation on clean data, range checks, format checks that require the correct type. Example: validating a date is in the future — use `mode="after"` so `v` is a `date` object, not a string. Validating multiple date string formats — use `mode="before"` so you can handle the raw string.

**Q3. How do you validate one field based on the value of another field?**

> **5-Year Exp Answer:**
> Use `@model_validator(mode="after")` — it has access to all fields as `self.field_name`:
>
> ```python
> @model_validator(mode="after")
> def check_dates(self) -> "MyModel":
>     if self.end_date <= self.start_date:
>         raise ValueError("end_date must be after start_date")
>     return self
> ```
>
> For `mode="before"` (raw dict), access other fields via `data["field_name"]`. In `@field_validator` (v2), use `info.data` to access previously-validated fields:
>
> ```python
> @field_validator("confirm_password")
> @classmethod
> def passwords_match(cls, v: str, info) -> str:
>     if "password" in info.data and v != info.data["password"]:
>         raise ValueError("Passwords must match")
>     return v
> ```
>
> Important: `info.data` only contains fields validated BEFORE this one — field order matters! That's why `@model_validator(mode="after")` is usually cleaner for complex cross-field logic.

**Q4. How do you return a transformed value from a validator?**

> **5-Year Exp Answer:**
> Simply `return` the transformed value from the validator — Pydantic uses the returned value as the field's value:
>
> ```python
> @field_validator("email")
> @classmethod
> def normalize_email(cls, v: str) -> str:
>     return v.strip().lower()  # ← transformed value stored
>
> @field_validator("tags", mode="before")
> @classmethod
> def parse_tags(cls, v) -> list:
>     if isinstance(v, str):
>         return [t.strip() for t in v.split(",")]  # str → list
>     return v
> ```
>
> If you don't return (return `None` implicitly), the field becomes `None`! This is a common bug. Always explicitly return the value (transformed or original) from validators. To reject: raise `ValueError("message")`. The exception message becomes the validation error message.

**Q5. How do you raise multiple validation errors from a single validator?**

> **5-Year Exp Answer:**
> Single `raise ValueError("message")` gives one error. For multiple errors, collect them and raise once:
>
> ```python
> @field_validator("password")
> @classmethod
> def validate_password(cls, v: str) -> str:
>     errors = []
>     if len(v) < 8:       errors.append("min 8 chars")
>     if not any(c.isupper() for c in v): errors.append("needs uppercase")
>     if not any(c.isdigit() for c in v): errors.append("needs digit")
>     if errors:
>         raise ValueError(f"Password requirements: {', '.join(errors)}")
>     return v
> ```
>
> In Pydantic v2, you can also use `PydanticCustomError` for more control over error types and codes. For model validators returning multiple field errors, raise `ValueError` as a list — Pydantic converts it to multiple errors:
>
> ```python
> @model_validator(mode="after")
> def validate_all(self):
>     from pydantic import ValidationError
>     # Multiple errors: collect as list of {loc, msg} dicts
>     # then raise ValueError — Pydantic formats them properly
>     raise ValueError([{"loc": ("field1",), "msg": "error1"},
>                       {"loc": ("field2",), "msg": "error2"}])
> ```

options: 5-Year Exp Answer: > Pydantic handles nested models automatically.

5-Year Exp Answer: > A dataclass is a Python decorator (@dataclass) introduced in Python 3.7 (PEP 557) that automatically generates boilerplate special methods for…
quiz.explanation: 5-Year Exp Answer: A dataclass is a Python decorator (@dataclass) introduced in Python 3.7 (PEP 557) that automatically generates boilerplate special methods for classes whose primary purpose is storing data. By default it generates: __init__() (constructor with all fields as parameters), __repr__() (human-readable string representation), and __eq__() (equality comparison that compares all fields).

quiz.question: What is the difference between a dataclass and a regular Python class?
options: 5-Year Exp Answer: > extra="forbid" raises ValidationError if the input contains any fields not defined in the model.
5-Year Exp Answer: > Circular references (A → B → A) require forward references: > > > > For true circular (A→B→A, not just self), use from __future__ import annotations…
5-Year Exp Answer: > Regular Enum members use identity comparison — two members are equal only if they're the same member.
5-Year Exp Answer: > A regular Python class requires you to manually write __init__, __repr__, __eq__ and other dunder methods.
quiz.explanation: 5-Year Exp Answer: A regular Python class requires you to manually write __init__, __repr__, __eq__ and other dunder methods. A dataclass auto-generates them from field annotations. Key differences: (1) Dataclasses require type annotations for all fields — they're not just code style, they're part of the dataclass specification.

quiz.question: What is __post_init__() and when do you use it?

5-Year Exp Answer: > __post_init__() is a special method automatically called by the dataclass-generated __init__() AFTER all field assignments are complete.
quiz.explanation: 5-Year Exp Answer: __post_init__() is a special method automatically called by the dataclass-generated __init__() AFTER all field assignments are complete. Use it for: (1) Validation — check field values and raise errors: if self.age < 0: raise ValueError("Age cannot be negative"). (2) Computed fields — derive field values from others: self.full_name = f"{self.first_name} {self.last_name}".
